genre: Texas psychedelic rock — self-described "mood-punk / cozmic soul"; groove- and synth-forward, danceable
show_time: 7:00pm — Visit Cincy Friday Night Nationals (SET 1 of 2)
artist_profile: The Bright Light Social Hour — Austin, TX five-piece, on the road behind Emergency Leisure (2023, their own Escondido Sound label). Wikipedia files them as psychedelic rock; their own EPK sells it as "mood-punk/cozmic soul" and quotes Consequence of Sound calling the record "a lush, space-western odyssey" and the Denver Post on "surreal, dreamlike… take me right to bed vocals." The Austin Chronicle's review lands the practical description: "dance-flavored melodies, shimmering retro soul, and sing-along anthems." Live lineup matches the input sheet exactly — Jackie O'Brien (bass/vocals, ch 26), Curtis Roush (guitar/vocals, ch 25), Mia Carruthers (keys/vocals, ch 27), Zac Catanzaro (drums), Juan Alfredo Ríos (percussion — the three congas and the accessory table, ch 20–23). What it means for the mix: this is a GROOVE band wearing psych clothing. The bass and the percussion rig carry the dance floor, the guitar and synths are layered texture rather than solo voices, and the three vocals blend as parts rather than stacking behind one lead. Press consistently describes the vocals as sitting IN the wash, not on top of it — so the vocal job here is separation between three voices, not pushing one forward.

reconciliation: No web/KB disagreements on any of the 17 units — every capsule fact found externally matched the mic-library row it was cross-checked against.

One refinement rather than a conflict: the e609's presence peak reads WIDER on the web (3-6 kHz, SoundMaximum) than the KB's 4-5 kHz. The trim is placed at 4000, inside both readings, and the difference is offered as a KB write-back rather than silently applied.
Noted so it isn't oversold: the Audix D4 row in the KB was itself corrected from this same RecordingHacks source on 2026-07-30, so that unit is a cross-check, not an independent confirmation.
kb_writeback: mic-library e609 row: widen the stated presence peak from 4-5 kHz to 3-6 kHz per Sennheiser spec + SoundMaximum.
eq-starting-points: no conga row exists — the 200/400/700 Hz + 5 kHz slap map and the size-based slotting method are write-back candidates.
eq-starting-points: the backline-vs-input-sheet tom mismatch (a D2 on a 16" floor tom) and the below-the-bump low bell that fixes it.

room_context: Fountain Square open-air: no room gain, nothing returns from the plaza — the L-Acoustics A15 mains and the delayed KS21 arch carry everything, and the downtown noise floor sits underneath. FSQ cuts run DEEPER than indoor (−6 to −9 typical, −10 on mud/box) and clarity is the whole game. TWO deliberate departures from that rule, both reasoned rather than forgotten: (1) where a capsule has ALREADY scooped a region — the Beta 52A's low-mids, the D2's 500Hz–1kHz dip, the SM57's 300–600Hz dip — the cut is held to −4/−6, because deep-cutting a baked scoop is the capsule gate running in reverse; (2) the keys channels (17/18/19/24) are capped at −6 rather than −8/−9, because this band's "shimmering retro soul" warmth is a feature and the mud the FSQ rule exists to fight outdoors is MECHANICAL — box, stage bleed, cab resonance — not room buildup, since an open plaza has none of its own. WEATHER (fetched, not assumed — Open-Meteo for the real show window): 77.5°F and 82% RH at the 7pm downbeat, climbing to 94% RH by 20:00 and holding 92% through the set, with gusts of 19 mph at downbeat and 25–35% shower probability all evening. Saturated air stops absorbing high frequencies over the throw, so the top end reaches the back of the plaza essentially intact — which INVERTS the usual outdoor call: there is no HF boost anywhere on this show, every baked presence peak is trimmed instead (i5 5.5k, Beta 27 5.5k/9k, e609 3–6k, SM57 6–7k, e604 3–5k), and the genre-reflex 8–10kHz shimmer lift on hats and cymbals becomes a CUT. Because the humidity keeps climbing across the set, every vocal de-esser is DYNAMIC rather than static — a top-end value dialled at 7pm is wrong by 10pm. The 19 mph gusts put the overhead pair at HPF 300 (a previous FSQ build at 22–28 mph needed 400; this is the lighter case). Shower risk is live all evening — worth having the contingency in mind.
style_note: Austin psych five-piece — groove-first, synth- and percussion-heavy, three-part vocals sitting inside the wash rather than over it.

Q: ch 25/26/27 vocals — wired or wireless? -> Brian: 'yes all wired mics'. Wired SM58s on stands; faders 33-36 untouched for this set.
Q: ch 24 'Pad' — what is it? -> Brian: SPD pad. Treated as finished audio: cuts only, one venue trim, no shaping.

Backline read from Brian's Backstage Backline quote 26-0645: DW Collectors maple kit, LP Classic conga trio, Fender Twin Reverb RI + Blues Deluxe, Ampeg SVT-CL / 410HLF / SVT 15e. J Roddy uses the SAME kit (Brian).
Blank-mic channels (14/15/16 and 28-32) stay template spares — not inputs.
LOCKER FORK L1 (ch 12 bass cab): SM57 as specified vs Shure PG52. RAISED, awaiting Brian — built to the sheet.
LOCKER FORK L2 (ch 20-22 congas): e604 x3 as specified vs DPA 4099 x3. RAISED, awaiting Brian — built to the sheet.

LOCKER FORK L3 (ch 25-27 vocals): SM58 as specified vs Beta 58A, contingent on wired Beta 58As existing (the four house capsules are on the wireless packs J Roddy needs). RAISED, awaiting Brian — built to the sheet.
Deliverables: two separate .ses files to load at the changeover, plus one combined MASTER carrying the changeover sheet between the two packets.
changes: BACKLINE vs INPUT SHEET MISMATCH — ch 7 is NOT a second rack tom. The quote ships ONE rack (10"x13") and TWO floor toms (14"x16" and 16"x18"), so ch 6 = 13" rack, ch 7 = 16" FLOOR tom, ch 8 = 18" floor tom. Ch 7 is built as a floor tom on a mic meant for small/mid toms.

TEMPLATE GATE (inherited, not written by this build): faders 6/7/8 ship the console's NATIVE gate enabled — thr -36.2 dB, release 227 ms — with sidechain bands re-tuned per drum in the 2026-08-01 template: Rack 1 217-262 Hz, Rack 2 153-242 Hz, Floor 96-116 Hz. *** Ch 7 is physically a 16" FLOOR tom on this backline, so its 153-242 Hz sidechain is listening in a rack-tom band — drop it toward 100-160 Hz at soundcheck or the gate will chatter on the wrong content. *** Ch 6 (13" rack) and ch 8 (18" floor) sidechains suit their drums as shipped.

Ch 7 gets +3 @ 100 to compensate for the D2's documented 'leaner deep lows than D4' on a 16" floor tom. The better mic is the D4, but there is only one and it is committed to the 18" — so the shortfall is handled in EQ and named here rather than papered over.

NO HF BOOST ANYWHERE on this show — the fetched 82->94% RH means saturated air delivers the top end intact, so every baked presence peak is trimmed instead. The genre-reflex 9kHz shimmer lift on hat (ch 5) and overheads (ch 9) is INVERTED into a cut.
Overheads HPF 300 driven by the fetched 19 mph gusts, not by taste.

Kick de-stack: BOTH mics carry an attack emphasis (91A 4-9kHz baked, 52A +7dB @4kHz). The 52A's 4k is trimmed -4 so the 91A owns the attack lane outright; the 91A's 200Hz is cut so the 52A owns the body. No stacked boost, top or bottom.

Beta 52A gets NO low bell, deliberately: the 24" kick's ~75Hz fundamental sits inside the capsule's baked big-low region, so a boost there would stack a voiced peak. Weight comes from the capsule plus the KS21 arch.
Bass low bell placed at 50Hz rather than the reflex 70-80, specifically to clear the 24" kick's ~75Hz fundamental.
Bass DI / bass cab lane split: DI owns everything below 150Hz, SM57 high-passed at 150 and owning 1-3kHz grind. Forum consensus is unanimous that a 57 on bass is a blend mic only.

SM57 box cuts (ch 12, ch 19) held LIGHT at -4/-6 against the FSQ deep-cut rule, because Shure's published curve has a dip at 300-600Hz already — cutting deep into a baked scoop is the capsule gate in reverse.

Congas slotted rather than copied: each drum is cut on its own ring (250/200/160) and its own harmonic (700/550/450), HPFs stepped 180/140/110 to match the Quinto/Conga/Tumba fundamentals from the backline quote. The 5kHz slap boost every source recommends is REFUSED — the e604 already emphasises 3-5kHz by +3dB.
Three vocals slotted by voice type on all four axes — HPF 90/85/110, de-ess 8000/7500/9000, nasal cut 1600/1200/2200, box 400/350/450 — so the three-part harmonies don't mask each other.

TEMPLATE OVERRIDE, ch 25/26/27: the FSQ template ships faders 25-36 at HPF 184 with a -18dB @5024Hz Q20 feedback notch (read directly from the installed template). Every HPF here overrides the 184 (far too high for these voices) and writing any B4 REMOVES the notch. RING OUT ALL THREE AT SOUNDCHECK.
Keys channels (17/18/19/24) capped at -6 rather than the full FSQ depth — retro-soul warmth is a feature, and outdoor mud is mechanical rather than room buildup.
Ch 17/18 are a STEREO keyboard across two MONO template faders — pan hard L/R, gain-match, identical EQ.
Ch 24 Pad, ch 17/18 keys and ch 19 keys amp are all TOUR-flagged: the backline quote's Keyboard line is a two-tier X-stand and nothing else ($0.00), so keyboards and keys amp are artist-supplied.
KB write-back offered, not silently applied: the e609's presence peak reads wider on the web (3-6kHz per SoundMaximum) than the KB's 4-5kHz. Trim placed at 4000, inside both readings.

reverbs.why: Transparent glue for when the plaza feels too dry between songs. Zero modulation means it disappears into the sources instead of adding a character of its own.

reverb_pairing: Vocal Plate is the default send on all three voices for the whole set — it is the one that keeps a groove tune moving. Sun Plate A is the psych send: bring it up on the dreamy, spacious material where the band wants the wash, and pull the Plate back as you do rather than stacking them. Sunset Chamber is held for the one big anthem moment; it is a different room, not a bigger plate, which is why the three complement rather than duplicate. Guitar Room sits under ch 13 on feature passages only and is deliberately short so it does not compete with whichever vocal send is up. Studio B Close runs low and constant under the kit and congas. Studio A sits under everything at a trickle. FSQ posture per the KB: start near factory decay, Late at −6, keep the rolloffs bright — the plaza adds nothing of its own, and at 92% RH it is not taking anything away either.

channels.mic_notes: Half-cardioid boundary lying inside the shell. Shure/RecordingHacks: the contour switch 'cuts 7dB at 400Hz' and the flat setting carries 'an emphasis from 4kHz to about 9kHz' for attack — so the beater click is already in the capsule. Known weakness is shell boxiness at 300-500. SWITCH STATE: contour assumed FLAT, so the 400Hz cut lives on the desk — if you find it engaged at load-in, halve the desk cut to about -4. LANE: this mic owns the ATTACK, CH2 owns the BODY.
channels.eq_summary: The 4-9kHz attack emphasis is the capsule's, not mine, so -3 @ 6300 just takes the edge off it before saturated air delivers it whole to the back of the plaza. -8 @ 400 is the full FSQ depth on the shell box this boundary mount always picks up. -5 @ 200 keeps this channel out of the low end entirely so CH2 owns the weight — on a dance-floor band the kick has to be felt, and that only works if one mic is making the weight instead of two arguing about it. HPF 60 for the same reason.

channels.name: Kick Out
channels.notes: Two-mic kick with CH1 — 52A at the port. Same VCA, pan together, polarity-check the pair in mono.
channels.mic_notes: Purpose-voiced kick dynamic. Shure/DrumHelper/FrontEndAudio: 20Hz-10kHz with 'a low-Q, high-end boost of about +7dB, reaching its peak around 4kHz', plus baked big lows and scooped low-mids. DE-STACK: that 4kHz peak is a SECOND attack emphasis on top of CH1's 4-9kHz — stacking them is the classic two-mic kick failure, so it is trimmed here and CH1 keeps the lane. No low bell: the 24" shell's ~75Hz fundamental sits inside the capsule's own big low end.
channels.eq_summary: -4 @ 4000 turns this into a pure body mic — the beater lives on CH1 and nowhere else. -7 @ 350 rather than -9 because the capsule has already scooped the low-mids and digging into a scoop just hollows it out. Nothing added at the bottom on purpose: the 52A's low end plus the KS21 arch is the weight, and outdoors there is no room gain to fight, so the job here is clearing the cardboard in front of the drum rather than manufacturing sub.

channels.name: Snare Top
channels.notes: Backline supplies BOTH a 6.5"x14" and a 5.5"x14" DW Collectors maple snare on two stands — confirm which is the main at soundcheck. Gate light or not at all; ghost notes have to live.
channels.mic_notes: RecordingHacks + KB agree exactly: 'a +5dB peak at 150 Hz and a pronounced +9dB peak at 5,500 Hz', 50Hz-16kHz, 140dB SPL. The crack is baked in — the desk's job at 5.5k is a trim, never a boost. The 150Hz body lift is left alone rather than doubled with a low bell.
channels.eq_summary: The crack everyone reaches for at 5k is already +9dB in this capsule, so -4 @ 5500 is about stopping it turning brittle through the A15s in saturated air, not about adding anything. -8 @ 500 dumps the box at full FSQ depth. The 150Hz body stays untouched — this band is groove-first and a thin snare kills a dance floor faster than a dull one.

channels.name: Snare Btm
channels.notes: POLARITY FLIPPED against CH3 — set at soundcheck. Wires only; this channel is not a body source.
channels.mic_notes: RecordingHacks: 40-18,000Hz, proximity '+9dB @ 85Hz' at 5cm, 'High mids are emphasized, +3dB from 3-5kHz', flat high end through 15kHz. Wide-cardioid below 2kHz turning supercardioid above it. The wire detail is delivered by that 3-5kHz emphasis, so B4 stays flat.
channels.eq_summary: HPF 220 is doing most of the work here — at clip distance the capsule's +9dB proximity lift plus kick bleed is all that lives below it, and none of it belongs in the PA. -7 @ 400 clears the shell. Deliberately no top-end lift: the rattle is in the capsule, the backline's fresh snare-side head will be lively on its own, and at 92% RH it all arrives intact anyway.

channels.name: Hat
channels.notes: Cymbals are BAND-supplied — the backline quote states the rider does not request cymbals — so the actual hats are unknown and may differ from J Roddy's. LF filter assumed FLAT, pad assumed OUT.
channels.mic_notes: Ruler-flat SDC — RecordingHacks/Shure give 20Hz-20kHz 'flat response curve', 146dB max SPL, 16.0dB(A) self-noise, and soundref calls it 'one of the flattest-sounding cardioids ever made'. Nothing is baked in, so everything you hear is the hat and the bleed. Takes EQ well precisely because it adds none of its own.
channels.eq_summary: HPF 500 per the hat rule — everything under it is bleed and there is no room outdoors to lose. The interesting move is -2 @ 9000: on a flat mic an air lift would normally be the one defensible boost, but the forecast is 94% RH by 8pm, and saturated air hands the whole top end to the back of the plaza — so the shimmer lift inverts into a small trim. Kept to -2 rather than the -4 J Roddy gets, because this band is danceable and the hat riding the time is part of what people move to. -6 @ 800 clears snare-bleed clank the cardioid pattern won't reject.

channels.name: Rack 1
channels.notes: Backline ships ONE rack tom (10"D x 13"W on a DW9900 mount) — this is it. Gate release matched to the kit's decay if gated at all. Template ships a native gate here: thr -36.2 dB, rel 227 ms, sidechain 217-262 Hz — suits a 13" rack, leave it.
channels.mic_notes: RecordingHacks: 44-18,000Hz hypercardioid, 144dB, 'a scooped-mids EQ curve, with a larger low-frequency boost than the D4'. KB puts the bump at ~150Hz with a 500Hz-1kHz dip. A low bell at 150 was drafted and REMOVED — that is exactly where the capsule's own boost sits, so it would have been a boost stacked on a voiced region.
channels.eq_summary: -6 @ 500 rather than the -8 the FSQ rule would ask for, because the capsule already dips through 500-1k and digging into a scoop just makes the drum disappear. -5 @ 300 takes the mud. Nothing added anywhere: on a 13" rack the D2's low bump is landing right on the drum's own fundamental, so it is already doing the job I would otherwise be asking the desk to do.

channels.name: Rack 2
channels.notes: NOT a second rack tom. The backline quote ships one 13" rack and TWO floor toms (14"x16" and 16"x18"), so this channel is the 16" FLOOR tom on legs, mic'd with a small/mid-tom mic. Built as a floor tom. Template ships a native gate here with a 153-242 Hz sidechain, tuned for a RACK tom. This is a 16" FLOOR tom — move the sidechain down toward 100-160 Hz at soundcheck.
channels.mic_notes: Same D2 capsule as CH6 but on a much bigger drum. The KB's flagged weakness — 'leaner deep lows than D4' — is exactly the problem here: a 16" floor tom's fundamental sits near 100Hz, BELOW the capsule's ~150Hz bump, on the falling side of the curve. That is what makes the low bell legitimate rather than lazy: it places weight where the mic runs out, it does not reinforce what the mic already does. The genuinely better mic is the D4, but there is only one and the 18" floor has it.
channels.eq_summary: +3 @ 100 puts back the bottom octave this pairing loses — the one boost on the kit, and it clears the capsule gate because 100Hz is below the D2's voiced region rather than on top of it. -6 @ 500 and -6 @ 300 clear box and mud, both held one step off full FSQ depth for the same scoop reason as CH6. HPF 65 rather than 90 because this drum needs its fundamental.

channels.name: Floor
channels.notes: The 16"D x 18"W floor tom on three DW legs — the big one. Template ships a native gate here: thr -36.2 dB, rel 227 ms, sidechain 96-116 Hz — suits the 18" floor tom, leave it.
channels.mic_notes: RecordingHacks reading Audix's CURRENT chart: '+6dB at 5kHz' with 'a secondary peak above 10kHz' and 'a low-frequency rolloff below 70Hz'. The old spec showed something different, which is why the KB row was corrected in July — the trap is adding click at 5k straight onto a baked peak. Not doing that. The 80Hz bell is the KB's own instruction: 'restore weight ~80Hz rather than expecting sub reach'.
channels.eq_summary: -4 @ 5000 trims the baked peak; at 92% RH both that peak and the secondary one above 10k arrive whole, so this is the only sensible direction. +3 @ 80 sits right where an 18" floor tom's fundamental meets the capsule's documented rolloff knee — placing weight where the mic gives up, with nothing asked of it below 70 because the KS21 arch owns that. -7 @ 400 takes the boom at FSQ depth. Punctuation drum in this band, so it stays controlled rather than ringing.

channels.name: Overheads
channels.notes: STEREO channel — both OH mics on this one fader. Never split onto fader 10 (SNARE PL8 return). HPF switch assumed OUT, -15dB pad assumed OUT. Cymbals are band-supplied and change at the band break.
channels.mic_notes: RecordingHacks: flat 'from ~60Hz to 3kHz', two HF peaks of '+2dB or less' at 5500Hz and 9kHz, supercardioid 'extremely consistent below 6400Hz' with deep 120-degree nulls. Onboard HPF options are -6dB/oct @115Hz or -18dB/oct @80Hz — both assumed OUT, so the 300Hz high-pass is the desk's.
channels.eq_summary: HPF 300 is set by the weather, not by taste: Open-Meteo has gusts at 19 mph at downbeat, and the overhead pair is the most wind-exposed input on the stage. -3 @ 9000 trims the upper of the two baked peaks — with 92% RH there is no air loss to excuse leaving it up, let alone adding to it. -7 @ 500 clears shell and stand wash that the supercardioid pattern still lets through, held off full depth because the capsule is flat through there and over-cutting would hollow the kit out.

channels.name: Bass DI
channels.notes: Confirm at load-in whether the DI is pre-amp or off the SVT-CL's balanced out — post-head it is already SVT-voiced and the 300Hz cut can come back a step. Mono/polarity check against CH12.
channels.mic_notes: Whirlwind/Sweetwater: '20Hz-20kHz ±1dB', -20dB loss, 133:1 ratio, TRHL transformer. Flat within a dB across the whole band, which is what clears both boosts here — there is no baked peak anywhere for them to stack on. LANE: this channel owns everything below 150Hz; CH12 is high-passed at 150 and cannot reach it.
channels.eq_summary: +3 @ 800 is the note-definition move, and it is the one this band actually needs — the basslines are syncopated and build tension through rhythm, which is unreadable outdoors if only the fundamental gets to the back of the plaza. +3 @ 50 places the weight, deliberately at 50 rather than the reflex 70-80 so it clears the 24" kick's ~75Hz fundamental instead of fighting it. -7 @ 300 takes the mud at full FSQ depth. Note the 800Hz boost is not an HF move, so the humidity rule doesn't reach it — that governs above about 4k, which is why B4 stays flat.

channels.name: Bass Mic
channels.notes: LOCKER FORK RAISED — SM57 as specified vs Shure PG52; built to the sheet pending Brian. Confirm which cab is mic'd (410HLF or 15e) for the patch sheet. Mono/polarity check against CH11.
channels.mic_notes: Shure's published curve (user guide v3.6, 2025-A): presence peak at 6-7kHz, +5 to +7dB — NOT 3-5kHz — reached by a ramp from ~2kHz that is only about +2dB by 3kHz; about -10dB at 40Hz; and a small dip at 300-600Hz. The forums are unanimous that this is a blend mic on bass: 'the SM57 has a low-end roll-off at about 200hz', and 'if you're just mic'ing, then use something else' (TalkBass/HomeRecording/PSW). The 410HLF's 1" compression driver also runs 'up to 4kHz', so there is real HF energy in front of it. LANE: grind only, 1-3kHz; CH11 owns the bottom.
channels.eq_summary: HPF 150 is the whole strategy — this mic physically cannot deliver the bottom of a cab that reaches 28Hz, so asking it to just doubles the mud. +3 @ 1600 is the growl, sitting on the flat part of the 57's ramp well below its peak. -4 @ 6500 trims that peak before it turns fizzy, which matters more than usual with a horn-loaded cab in saturated air. -4 @ 400 only, not the -7 the FSQ rule would ask for, because Shure's own curve already dips through 300-600 — cutting deep into a baked scoop is the same mistake as boosting into a baked peak.

channels.name: Guitar 1
channels.instrument: Electric guitar cab — Fender '65 Twin Reverb RI (Curtis)
channels.notes: e609 has no clip mount — hung over the cab face by its cable, the way it is designed to work. Backline supplies both a '65 Twin Reverb RI and a Blues Deluxe RI; built for the Twin. Confirm at load-in.
channels.mic_notes: Sennheiser spec 40Hz-15kHz supercardioid; SoundMaximum puts the voicing as 'a 3-6,000 Hz midrange peak' and the silver has a reputation for going 'thin, harsh, and brittle at times'. The KB reads that peak narrower (4-5kHz) — offered as a KB refinement rather than silently diverging, and the trim is placed at 4000 which sits inside both readings. The amp compounds it: the '65 Twin Reverb RI is 85W through two 12" Jensen C-12Ks with blackface voicing and a bright switch — bright on top of bright.
channels.eq_summary: -5 @ 4000 is the deepest presence trim on this band, and it earns it: the e609's baked peak, the Twin's bright blackface voicing and 92% RH are three bright things in series with nothing to absorb any of them. -6 @ 900 and -7 @ 300 go after exactly what the psych-mixing sources warn about — layered fuzz and modulation 'turn murky quickly, burying clarity under low-end and midrange haze'. What survives is the 1.5-3kHz body, which is where the guitar's actual character lives in this band; it is texture inside a wash, not a solo voice, so clearing space for it matters more than making it loud.

channels.name: Key 1 L
channels.notes: STEREO keyboard across two MONO faders — pan hard L with CH18 hard R, gain-matched, identical EQ. Keyboard is artist-supplied (backline quote's Keyboard line is a two-tier X-stand only).
channels.mic_notes: IMP 2 is flat to ±1dB, so nothing here is the DI's doing — what arrives is a finished, produced patch, and the voicing decision was made upstream by whoever built it. Same posture as a cab-sim'd direct feed: cuts only, one venue trim, no corrective shaping.
channels.eq_summary: -6 @ 300 rather than the full FSQ -8 or -9, and the reason is on paper: this band's warmth is a feature, not a defect, and outdoors the mud the deep-cut rule exists to fight is mechanical — box, bleed, cab resonance — because an open plaza contributes none of its own. -5 @ 1500 is about real estate, not tone: the synth layers and the three vocals want the same space, and the keys have more of it to give. B4 stays flat because none of the top end here is mine to shape.

channels.name: Key 1 R
channels.notes: Pair with CH17 — pan hard R, gain-matched, identical EQ. Artist-supplied keyboard.
channels.mic_notes: Identical to CH17 by design — a stereo source split across two mono faders has to be matched or the image walks as the part moves. Flat DI, finished audio arriving, cuts only.
channels.eq_summary: Same curve as CH17 deliberately. Any difference between the two channels would show up as the keyboard drifting across the stereo field on sustained pads, which is the one thing a psych band's synth wash cannot survive.

channels.name: Key Amp
channels.notes: Amp is artist-supplied — not on the backline quote. Confirm model at load-in. If it comes up harsh, move the mic off the cone centre before reaching for EQ.
channels.mic_notes: Same corrected Shure curve as CH12 — 6-7kHz peak at +5 to +7dB, small dip at 300-600Hz. Amp model unknown, which makes placement the first lever rather than EQ: the cone centre is 'the brightest, most aggressive sound with the most high-frequency content', the edge is darker, and the standard fix for harshness at 3k is moving off centre (Sweetwater / Dinosaur Rock Guitar).
channels.eq_summary: -4 @ 6500 sits on the 57's baked peak; an amped keyboard patch is already bright and saturated air delivers all of it, so trimming is the only defensible direction. -5 @ 1200 keeps the amp out of the vocals' way — deeper than the DI's 1500 cut on purpose, so the two keys sources are not cutting the same hole. -6 @ 350 held light for the capsule's own 300-600 dip.

channels.name: Conga L
channels.notes: Highest of the three. Drum order assumed Quinto/Conga/Tumba left to right per the standard LP trio layout — CONFIRM AT SOUNDCHECK; if the player sets up mirrored, these three cards move with the DRUMS, not the channel numbers. LOCKER FORK RAISED (e604 vs DPA 4099) — built to the sheet.
channels.mic_notes: e604: proximity '+9dB @ 85Hz' at 5cm and 'High mids are emphasized, +3dB from 3-5kHz' (RecordingHacks). That 3-5kHz emphasis matters here more than anywhere else on the show, because the conga slap sits at 5kHz (AudioRecording.me) — so the slap is ALREADY in the capsule and the standard 5k boost is refused. An 11" quinto tunes around F3-D4, so its ring is the highest of the three.
channels.eq_summary: Cut on this drum's OWN frequencies, not the section's: -6 @ 250 is the quinto's ring and -6 @ 700 its harmonic, both higher than the other two congas because the drum is. HPF 180 sits above its fundamental and kills the +9dB proximity boom that three clip mics would otherwise pile into the arch. Nothing added up top — the slap is the capsule's, and at 92% RH it reaches the back of the plaza without help.

channels.name: Conga C
channels.notes: Middle drum. Order confirm at soundcheck with CH20/CH22.
channels.mic_notes: Same capsule as CH20/CH22, different drum. The published conga map puts the fundamental 'around 200Hz' with harmonics 'notably at 400Hz and 700Hz' and resonance at 200-240Hz — this middle drum is the one that sits closest to that textbook centre, which is why it takes the deepest ring cut of the three.
channels.eq_summary: -7 @ 200 is the deepest of the three ring cuts because this drum's fundamental lands squarely in the plaza's worst congestion, right where bass and kick are also working. -6 @ 550 takes its harmonic. HPF 140 steps down from the quinto's 180 to match the lower fundamental. Cutting all three congas at a shared 200Hz would have hollowed the tumba and missed the quinto entirely — that stepping IS the separation.

channels.name: Conga R
channels.notes: Lowest of the three. Order confirm at soundcheck with CH20/CH21.
channels.mic_notes: The 12.5" tumba is the low voice of the trio and the one the e604's 'modest low end' serves worst — which is why the HPF comes down to 110 rather than following the others up. Same +3dB 3-5kHz slap emphasis baked in as CH20/CH21.
channels.eq_summary: -7 @ 160 sits on this drum's own ring, well below where the other two are cut. -5 @ 450 is the shallowest harmonic cut of the three because the tumba has the least to spare up there. HPF 110 is the lowest of the trio so the drum keeps its bottom — it is the one carrying the low end of the percussion rig, and a dance-floor band needs that. No slap boost, same as its neighbours.

channels.name: Aux Perc
channels.notes: One mic over a table of small bright sources — tambourine, shakers, blocks, bells. LF filter assumed FLAT, pad assumed OUT.
channels.mic_notes: Second of the two SM81s (the other is the hat). Ruler-flat, 146dB max SPL, nothing baked — so unlike every other channel on this show there is no capsule peak arguing against a lift here. The reason there still isn't one is purely the weather. The mic is also pointed straight at a 24"x24" flat table, which contributes its own box tone around 1kHz on every hit.
channels.eq_summary: -4 @ 9000 is the same inversion as the hat and it has to stay consistent with it: a flat mic plus saturated air means trim, not add. A tambourine's whole voice lives up there and at 92% RH all of it reaches the back of the plaza — through an A15 array that is an ice pick. -5 @ 1000 is the accessory table itself, not the instruments. HPF 250 buys rejection against kick and conga bleed arriving across the table, which is worth more here than any low end this channel could contribute.

channels.name: Pad
channels.notes: Confirmed by Brian as an SPD pad. Artist-supplied. Landing on ONE mono fader — if the samples are stereo-wide they will sum; check at soundcheck.
channels.mic_notes: The purest finished-audio source on the show — produced samples arriving through a flat DI. Every tonal decision was made by whoever loaded the kit, exactly like a cab-sim'd direct out, so the honest posture is one venue trim and nothing else. HPF only 40 because sampled sub content is often the point of a pad in this kind of set.
channels.eq_summary: One move: -5 @ 300 to keep the samples from stacking mud onto a stage that already has bass, kick, congas and synth in that region. Nothing else touched — shaping a finished sample means fighting a decision someone already made deliberately, and if it needs more than this it is a level problem, not an EQ problem.

channels.name: Curtis
channels.notes: Wired, on a stand, in front of his own amp. TEMPLATE OVERRIDE — writing B4 removes the template's -18dB @5024Hz Q20 feedback notch and the HPF overrides the template's 184Hz. RING OUT AT SOUNDCHECK. LOCKER FORK RAISED (SM58 vs Beta 58A) — built to the sheet.
channels.mic_notes: Shure/RecordingHacks: 50-15,000Hz cardioid, 'frequency response tailored for vocals, with brightened midrange and bass rolloff'; the KB puts the presence at 4-6kHz and flags it going muddy worked close. Cuts only, every genre — feedback control, not taste. Slotted against CH26 and CH27 by voice type, not by hierarchy.
channels.eq_summary: -3 @ 8000 with a dynamic de-esser rather than a static cut, because the humidity climbs from 82% to 94% across the set — a value dialled at the 7pm downbeat is simply wrong by 10pm, and only a dynamic band tracks that. -4 @ 1600 is his nasal lane, deliberately different from Jackie's 1200 and Mia's 2200 so the three-part harmonies don't mask each other. -6 @ 400 is the box. HPF 90 sits in the 60-100Hz range that suits a male voice and, just as importantly, gets his own guitar amp out of a mic pointed at it.

channels.name: Jackie
channels.notes: Wired, on a stand, in front of the SVT rig. TEMPLATE OVERRIDE — B4 removes the -18 @5024 Q20 notch, HPF overrides 184. RING OUT AT SOUNDCHECK.
channels.mic_notes: Same SM58 capsule as CH25 and CH27 — so all the separation has to come from WHERE each voice is cut, which is the only lever a cuts-only rule leaves. This mic has the worst bleed situation of the three: it is pointed across an Ampeg SVT rig that reaches 28Hz.
channels.eq_summary: The lowest de-ess centre of the three at 7500 and the lowest nasal cut at 1200, giving the lower-sitting voice room where it lives and keeping it clear of Curtis at 1600. -6 @ 350 tracks his chest register a little lower than Curtis's 400. HPF 85 is the lowest of the three vocals — low enough to keep the body of the voice, high enough to keep the SVT out of it.

channels.name: Mia
channels.notes: Wired, on a stand at the keyboard. TEMPLATE OVERRIDE — B4 removes the -18 @5024 Q20 notch, HPF overrides 184. RING OUT AT SOUNDCHECK.
channels.mic_notes: The one upper-register voice in the three-part blend, which is why every value on this channel sits above the other two rather than beside them. Same SM58 presence region baked in; same cuts-only rule.
channels.eq_summary: HPF 110 is the highest of the three, matching the 80-120Hz range that suits an upper voice and buying real rejection from the keyboard amp beside her. De-ess at 9000 — the highest centre, because this voice actually reaches up there and the other two don't. -4 @ 2200 puts her nasal cut a full octave above Jackie's, which is what stops the harmonies from turning into one blurred part. -7 @ 450 is the deepest box cut of the three; an upper voice can spare it, and outdoors that region is where three open vocal mics gang up.
